source.label: ETS TOEFL ITP Level 1 Practice Tests, Volume 3 — Practice Test A Listening Comprehension Script
source.note: Published Listening Comprehension Script from the owner-authorized source book.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Have you seen my calculator? It was right here a minute ago.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Did you look under your book? I’m always losing things that way.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I really wanna take astronomy, but my courseload this spring is too heavy already.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: The summer session might be a good idea, since you’ll be working on campus anyway.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Professor Clark, I’d like to repeat the experiment from last class. Is there a possibility I could use the lab over the weekend?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It’ll be locked, but you can get the key from the security office. Make sure you return it when you’re finished.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I really like your sweatshirt! I don’t think I’ve ever seen a design like that before.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yeah, it’s pretty cool, isn’t it? My parents were in Japan last year and brought it back for me.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Are you free tonight? I’m meeting a few friends at the restaurant on Main Street.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, I’d love to. But I already have dinner plans for tonight. Another time perhaps.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I just registered for the research conference—the deadline is tomorrow. It doesn’t take long though—you simply go to the conference Web site.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I guess I’d better do that today, huh? I have a little time before I teach my next class.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That’s a great bike! Where’d you get it?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You know that sporting goods store on Harrison Street–they’ve been running tremendous sales all summer!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: So, how much was your plane ticket?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: More than I could really afford—I had to dip into my savings.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Professor Jones, we had a power failure in my dorm last night, so I wasn’t able to finish my paper. Could I hand it in tomorrow?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I understand that things sometimes do come up, but I don’t make any exceptions. I made that clear in the first class… and the library was open till midnight…

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’m thinking of moving off-campus next semester, but since I don’t have a car, I’d need to stay pretty close by. Any suggestions?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: It just so happens the people who live downstairs from me are moving next month, so their apartment might be available, and it’s only a block away from the university. If you’re interested, I’ll look into it for you.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: What an awful movie! A total waste of time!

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You can say that again!

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I hear your sister got into a prestigious university. I bet she was checking her mail every day for her acceptance letter.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, she was a little nervous until she found out last week.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’m really sorry I’m late for the meeting. My car wouldn’t start, and I had to take the bus.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That’s okay. We’re still waiting for Mark.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Wow, you seem to be in a really good mood today. What’s the secret?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Dunno. I guess some mornings you wake up feeling great, and some mornings you don’t.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I’d think twice about taking a history class next year. There’s not a single good professor in the whole history department.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Look. That’s what you said last semester about the sociology department. And I’m very glad I didn’t pay any attention to what you said.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I know we’re supposed to meet at five in the library, but something came up unexpectedly. Would you mind changing it to six?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Not at all. My schedule’s very flexible.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Can you believe it? A 20-page term paper and a final exam. What does Professor Johnson think? That we don’t have any classes but his?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Wait a second. I’m sure he said it was either one or the other.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I’m really happy I got that athletic scholarship, but I’m embarrassed by the big fuss all my friends are making.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Well it is quite an accomplishment. Of course your friends are happy for you!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: My computer screen is flashing… and I can’t get it to stop.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, a similar thing happened to me the other day. I’ll bet together we can figure out what to do.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: There’s quite a crowd at the health center today. I’m surprised so many people are interested in getting a free blood pressure test.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Come to think of it, I haven’t had mine checked in a while. Guess I’ll go get in line…

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I can’t believe I actually graduated and I’m leaving tonight. I enjoyed studying with you this semester.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Same here. And hey—don’t forget to drop me a line once in a while. Let me know how the new job goes.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Look at the fancy pen I just found under this bench. It looks expensive.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh. So THAT’s where it went!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I don’t know what I was thinking of when I gave you those directions.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, don’t worry about it. I made it before the conference began. I didn’t have to drive that much out of my way.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Now that you’ve had a chance to read our proposal to renovate the campus café, do you think the university will approve it?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Actually, I’ve been so busy, I haven’t had a chance to look at it yet.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Wow, I’ve already taken one of those pills for my headache, but it’s still bothering me.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, why not take another? The recommended dose is one or two, depending on how bad it is.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: What’s Phil doing here? I thought he was taking the fall semester off.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Didn’t you hear that his parents talked him out of it?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: A florist told me that if I want to keep flowers looking fresh, I should cut a bit off the stems before putting them in water. I wonder if it really works…

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Someone told me the same thing and the bouquet I had did last longer. Anyway, it can’t hurt, can it?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: That was a fascinating lecture, but the questions from the audience afterward were mostly irrelevant to the topic!

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, I totally agree. I would’ve preferred less of that and more of the speaker.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: I just found out my dentist retired last month. Do you have one you’d recommend?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yeah. In fact, I have a checkup there next week. Say, I’ve even got his card with me, if you want to wait a minute while I get it out.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Tomorrow I have my big presentation in anthropology class… I’m really worried about speaking in front of the class.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You always say that, and then you always do really well. You have nothing to worry about.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: So how was the singing competition last weekend?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: You don’t wanna know.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: What d’ya mean? Wasn’t it near the beach?… That should’ve been fun!

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: It should’ve been fun, but we only came in second place… not only that, but we weren’t even really able to enjoy the beach either.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Hold on—you’re upset about finishing second? How many singing groups competed?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: About 30. I know second place sounds okay, but that’s three years in a row we’ve been in second, and it’s the same group that’s beaten us three years in a row.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That’s too bad… but what about the beach?… I ended up spending a lot of time studying in the library. I would have loved to be at the beach swimming in the ocean or playing beach volleyball instead of being stuck in the library studying.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Well, it wasn’t exactly like that. I had to spend some time studying, too. We really didn’t have much free time. We were scheduled almost the whole time—practicing, performing, or watching the competition.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: So you were that busy?

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yeah, but y’know the ocean water’s still cold, so I don’t think we really missed too much.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Well, maybe you guys should plan to go back when the semester’s over.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Yep, that’s exactly what we have in mind. It should be a lot more fun there when the weather warms up—and we don’t have to think about competing.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Professor, I really like those sculptures by Brancusi. They have such simple, elegant lines.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, they do.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Were there any other sculptors doing work like that?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Well, yes, there was a sculptor named Isamu Noguchi. Noguchi actually worked in Brancusi’s studio for a time, so Brancusi was one of several important influences on his work.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Okay…

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Noguchi was born in 1904, in California. His mother was an American writer, and his father was a Japanese poet… And during his childhood, Noguchi lived in Japan. And when his mother hired a carpenter to build a house there, Noguchi helped out, and in the process came to love working with wood and other natural materials.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Okay…

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Later, he returned to the United States and became an artist, then went to Paris, where he worked for Brancusi.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: So Brancusi taught him the art of sculpting?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes—and a commitment to strict economy in his art.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Economy?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Yes, but not in the usual financial sense. In this case, the term “economy” refers to stripping away unnecessary details, emphasizing the artwork’s basic form.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Oh, okay.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Also, after Noguchi had studied under Brancusi for awhile, he took a trip back to Japan. And on that trip, he studied some traditional Japanese gardens, and he noticed how stone was used to create a very simple, but elegant open space. So these gardens halfway around the world actually shared some of the defining characteristics of Brancusi’s sculptures.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: And probably reinforced and, like, further shaped the concept of economy in Noguchi’s mind.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Undoubtedly.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Senses play an important role in consumer decision-making. Shoppers like to… sniff a piece of fish… or listen to a stereo before buying it. But the power of touch was not fully understood by researchers until recently. Evidence is showing that consumers who’re able to handle merchandise are more likely to buy it—and pay more for it. Shoppers touch for various reasons. There’s fact-finding touch, like turning a food container to read the list of ingredients; or picking an item up to assess its specific attributes, such as weight, texture, or temperature. There’s also touch for its own sake… ’cause it feels nice to, say, run your fingers along a shiny table. Psychologically, touching an item fosters a sense of ownership, which makes it more difficult to resist buying it. So it makes sense when retailers display sweaters on shelves rather than in protective plastic bags. One unexpected finding of this research is that—in terms of generating sales—imagined touch is just as effective as actual touch. That’s good to know if you’re writing descriptions of items sold online! The need to touch varies; shoppers whose need to touch is high… they tend to buy more when touching is encouraged. In one experiment, researchers placed a “Feel the freshness” sign on a fruit display. All shoppers were more likely to touch the fruit when the sign was there than when it wasn’t. But shoppers who ranked higher in the need to touch were more likely to buy the fruit they touched.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Let me warn you against a mistake that historians often make— they sometimes assume that people in the past used the same concepts we do. There’s a wonderful example that made news in the history of mathematics a while ago. It concerns an ancient Mesopotamian tablet that had some calculations on it—sophisticated calculations that looked like measurements of triangles…so that’s what many historians assumed they were. And if the Mesopotamians knew how to use these calculations—and historians started thinking that they did—that meant their math was incredibly advanced. Well, it turns out that the idea that Mesopotamians used sophisticated methods to calculate the measurements of triangles is probably wrong. Why do we think that? Because we discovered that Mesopotamians didn’t know how to measure angles, which is a crucial element in the whole process of triangle calculations. Apparently the Mesopotamians had a number of other uses for the calculations on the tablet. These other uses were important, but they were not related to triangles. And so these tablets, in all likelihood, were practice sheets, if you like, for doing math exercises. In all likelihood, it was the ancient Greeks who first calculated the measurements of triangles. And this was hundreds of years after the Mesopotamians.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: A really surprising discovery was made up in Canada recently… some fossilized animal footprints they found in some sandstone there. So, why’s that exciting? Well, this sandstone is really old, and so the footprints are too—older, by about 40 million years they think, than any footprints ever found… of animals that walked on land. Since we believe that land animals originally emerged from the sea, well, this shows the move from sea to land happened way earlier than we thought—40 million years earlier—and that’s a lot. And finding these fossils was sheer luck. There were these Canadian stonecutters cutting up sandstone to use as a building material, and apparently this stone with the fossil prints wasn’t smooth enough to use. So the workers rejected it for building use, and the discarded stone lay there for years before anyone who could recognize its true importance… was lucky enough to lay eyes on it. Now how do we know these impressions were made by animals on land—not still back in the sea, walking on the seafloor? Well, the footprints look too deep to be made underwater… ‘cause underwater you’re buoyant and your footsteps’re lighter. So any tracks wouldn’t be as deep. But how could sea animals end up doing better by moving onto land? Well, the sea was full of dangerous predators that would attack their young. So one theory is that land offered them a safer place to reproduce—a greater chance to have their young survive.
